description: There Is Nothing Permament Except Change
summary:
SPHEREx maps the entire sky in 102 infrared colors and repeats the survey every six months, so every spot builds up a stack of images taken at different times. Nearby stars, brown dwarfs, asteroids and variable stars hide in those repeats, but the archive offers files, not a way to see change.

SPHEREx Blink is a web tool that turns any spot on the sky into a short movie. Type an object name or coordinates, and it finds every SPHEREx image of that spot, removes the zodiacal glow and bad pixels, aligns the images north-up, stacks the ones from each survey pass and blinks them, the same technique that found Pluto. Because each image samples a different wavelength, the same data also give a 0.75-5 µm spectrum and a light curve, so users can see what moves and learn what it is. The tool works on all five challenge targets, keeps running from NASA’s cloud copy of the data when the main archive is down, and makes every view a shareable link.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
SPHEREx maps the entire sky in 102 infrared colors, from 0.75 to 5 µm, and repeats the survey every six months. Every position on the sky therefore collects a growing stack of images taken at different times, and hidden in those repeats are objects that move or change: nearby stars, cold brown dwarfs, asteroids and variable stars. NASA's archive delivers these images as individual files, but it offers no easy way to see how the sky changes over time.
SPHEREx Blink closes that gap. You type an object name or coordinates, and in about a minute the tool turns that spot into a short movie built from real SPHEREx data. It is the same blink technique Clyde Tombaugh used to find Pluto: when images of the same field are played one after another, anything that moves or changes brightness jumps out to the eye.
The same images are also used a second way. Each SPHEREx image is taken at a slightly different wavelength, so the measurements that make the movie also give the object's spectrum and light curve. The movie tells you whether something moves or changes, and the spectrum tells you what it is. Methane absorption, for example, is the signature of a cold brown dwarf.

HOW IT WORKS
First, the object name is resolved with the CDS Sesame service, including the star's proper motion, and NASA's IRSA archive is searched for every SPHEREx image that covers the position. New weekly data releases show up automatically, with no change to the code. Next, the tool downloads only the small piece of each image it needs: instead of fetching whole 64 MB files, it reads just those bytes from NASA's public copy of the SPHEREx data on Amazon S3, with IRSA's cutout service as a backup.
Each cutout is then cleaned and aligned: the zodiacal light is subtracted, flagged pixels are masked, and every image is placed on a common north-up grid. The target's brightness is measured at its position on each image's date, so even fast-moving stars stay centered. Images are stacked per detector by survey pass, week, day or single exposure, and because each survey-pass frame covers the full wavelength range, the differences between frames come from time, not from color. Finally, the browser receives the stacked images as numbers and draws them itself, so contrast, colors and difference views change instantly.

FEATURES
You can play the movie with speed control, a timeline and keyboard shortcuts, and switch to difference views (against the first frame, the previous frame or the mean) or a deep sum of all frames. All six detectors can be shown together or one at a time. Spectra and light curves are available for the target or for any pixel you click. The field of view can be set from 1.8 to 18 arcminutes, and you can drag the image to look around while the target stays tracked.
Gaia DR3 stars can be overlaid, moved to each frame's date using their proper motions, and an Aladin Lite map shows the same field in 2MASS, AllWISE and DSS. Each frame lists its quality flags and how much of the field is affected by ghosts, halos or streaks. Every view has a shareable link and an embed mode, and frames can be downloaded as PNG or as FITS files with sky coordinates.

RESULTS ON THE FIVE CHALLENGE TARGETS
Barnard's Star moves 10 arcseconds north between September 2025 and August 2026; the difference image shows a clean blue and red pair, and the Gaia stars line up with the SPHEREx sources. Epsilon Indi B gives a textbook brown dwarf spectrum from 100 images, with methane absorption at 1.6 to 1.8, 2.2 to 2.5 and 3.3 µm, and carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide absorption at 4.3 to 4.7 µm. WISE 0855, the coldest known brown dwarf, is now about 2 arcminutes away from the 2010 coordinate given in the challenge, and the proper-motion tracking finds it automatically; as expected, it only appears beyond 3.8 µm, and its brightness matches the WISE measurements. RW Aurigae roughly doubles in brightness at 4 to 5 µm between survey passes. R Draconis sits in a deep field near the north ecliptic pole, where its 2,493 images are split into seven frames that show the star's pulsation.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT
SPHEREx Blink makes a brand-new NASA dataset usable for discovery without writing any code. Students and citizen scientists can look for moving and changing objects the way Backyard Worlds volunteers do with WISE data, and researchers get a fast first look at any position, with a spectrum and a light curve, before downloading anything. Because the tool reads the archive live, it keeps improving as SPHEREx keeps observing, and shareable links make every finding easy to discuss and check.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED
We apply the SPHEREx quality flags and report contamination rather than hiding it, and when an image has the target at the very edge of the detector, the tool swaps it for a better-placed one. Brightness is measured without aperture correction, so spectra are clearly labeled as relative. NASA's IRSA search service was down for much of the hackathon, so the tool falls back to saved image lists and reads pixels directly from NASA's S3 copy to keep working. Processed cutouts are cached, so smaller or shifted views of a field load without downloading again. For accessibility there are light and dark themes, keyboard shortcuts, a reduced-motion mode, and chart colors checked for color-blind readers.

TOOLS AND DATA
The backend is written in Python with FastAPI, astropy, astroquery, pyvo, reproject and NumPy. The frontend is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Aladin Lite. The data come from NASA SPHEREx Level 2 images through IRSA and its Amazon S3 copy, ESA Gaia DR3, and the CDS services SIMBAD, VizieR and Aladin.

NEXT STEPS
We want to add automatic detection of moving sources on difference images, a "flag this" button so citizen scientists can mark what they find, and GIF export so people can share their discoveries.
